question: What are the main components of the autopilot flight director system?

options.text: Two flight control computers and the mode control panel
A single flight control computer and the FMC
The mode control panel and the autothrottle computer
The FMC and the two air data computers

explanation: Two computers give the redundancy needed for a dual channel approach, and the mode control panel is the crew interface to both.

question: How many autopilot channels may be engaged during normal cruise flight?

options.text: Two, but only above 20000 ft
Either one or two at the crew discretion
Two
One

explanation: Single channel operation is the norm. The second channel is reserved for the approach, where its redundancy is actually needed.

question: Under what condition can both autopilot channels be engaged?

options.text: Whenever both flight directors are switched on
Whenever the flaps are extended
During an ILS approach with APP mode selected
During any instrument approach

explanation: Dual channel operation exists to provide redundancy during an automatic approach and landing, so it is tied to APP mode.

question: How is the second autopilot channel engaged for an approach?

options.text: By selecting both flight director switches to ON
By moving the disengage bar to the second detent
Automatically at 1500 ft radio altitude
By pressing the second CMD switch after APP mode is selected

explanation: The crew action is deliberate, so a dual channel approach can never be entered by accident during normal manoeuvring.

question: What is the essential difference between CMD and CWS?

options.text: CMD is used in flight and CWS only on the ground
CMD controls pitch only while CWS controls roll only
CMD follows the selected modes while CWS responds to pilot control forces
CMD uses computer A while CWS uses computer B

explanation: In CWS the pilot is still manoeuvring the airplane, but through the autopilot servos rather than directly.

question: What does the autopilot do in CWS when the pilot releases the control force?

options.text: It reverts to the previously selected CMD mode
It holds the attitude existing at the moment of release
It returns the airplane to wings level
It disengages automatically

explanation: Holding the resulting attitude is what makes CWS a manoeuvring mode rather than a navigation mode.

question: With CWS engaged in roll and the localizer armed, what happens as the airplane approaches the beam?

options.text: The autopilot disengages and the flight director takes over
The localizer arming is cancelled
Nothing, capture requires CMD to be engaged
The system captures the localizer and transitions to CMD

explanation: The capture logic remains active in this case, which is why an armed localizer can take control even with CWS selected in roll.

question: What is the minimum altitude for engaging the autopilot after takeoff?

options.text: 200 ft AGL
400 ft AGL
1000 ft AGL
1500 ft AGL

explanation: The limit gives the crew time to establish the airplane manually before handing over. Verify the exact figure against your operator FCOM.

question: By which two means can the autopilot be disengaged?

options.text: The go around switch or the stabiliser trim switches
The control wheel disengage switch or the autothrottle disengage switch
The control wheel disengage switch or the mode control panel disengage bar
The disengage bar or the flight director switches

explanation: One method is on the yoke within immediate reach, and the other is on the panel, so disengagement never depends on a single switch.

question: How does the autopilot disengage warning present itself?

options.text: A flashing red light and an aural warning
A master caution light on the forward panel
A steady amber light only
A single chime with no light

explanation: An unannounced disengagement is dangerous, so the warning is attention getting and has to be positively cancelled.

question: Which of the following is a roll mode?

options.text: LVL CHG
V/S
HDG SEL
ALT HOLD

explanation: Roll modes command the airplane about the longitudinal axis, while the others are pitch modes controlling the vertical path.

question: What is the range of the bank angle limit selector?

options.text: 5 to 25 degrees
10 to 25 degrees
10 to 30 degrees
15 to 35 degrees

explanation: A reduced limit gives a gentler turn at high altitude or for passenger comfort, at the cost of a larger turn radius.

question: Which mode is affected by the bank angle limit selector?

options.text: HDG SEL
VOR/LOC after capture
LNAV
All roll modes equally

explanation: The route based mode uses its own bank scheduling to fly the coded path, so a manual limit would prevent it tracking accurately.

question: In LVL CHG, what controls the airspeed?

options.text: The bank angle limit selector
Thrust, while pitch holds the vertical speed
The FMC vertical path
Pitch, while thrust is set to the climb limit or idle

explanation: Fixing the thrust and using pitch for speed is what makes the mode deliver the best available rate for the conditions.

question: In V/S mode, what controls the airspeed?

options.text: The selected vertical speed
The autothrottle
The FMC speed schedule
Pitch attitude

explanation: Pitch is committed to the vertical speed, so speed becomes the autothrottle task.

question: What is the principal hazard of using V/S at high altitude?

options.text: The selected rate may be unachievable and the speed will decay
The autopilot will revert to CWS in pitch
The autothrottle disconnects above the optimum altitude
The bank angle limit is automatically reduced

explanation: The mode will hold the vertical speed at the expense of airspeed, so an over ambitious selection near the performance ceiling leads to a low speed situation.

question: What does ALT HOLD do?

options.text: Levels the airplane and then reverts to V/S
Climbs to the altitude selected on the mode control panel
Holds the altitude selected in the FMC
Holds the altitude at which the mode engaged

explanation: It captures the current altitude, which is not necessarily the one selected on the panel.

question: How is the altitude acquire mode selected?

options.text: By pressing the altitude intervention switch
By setting the vertical speed to zero
It cannot be selected, it engages automatically approaching the selected altitude
By pressing the ALT HOLD switch twice

explanation: The transition from a climb or descent into level flight is automatic so that the level off is always flown to the same schedule.

question: What is the effect of changing the mode control panel altitude during altitude capture?

options.text: The capture may be interrupted and a new pitch mode must be selected
The autopilot disengages
The airplane immediately levels at the original altitude
Nothing until altitude hold has engaged

explanation: Changing the target during the capture removes the reference the mode was working towards, which is why the selection is made before the capture begins.

question: In VNAV, what does the FMC control?

options.text: Thrust only, with pitch flown manually
Roll and pitch, with thrust controlled manually
Both pitch and thrust to fly the vertical profile
Pitch only, with thrust controlled from the mode control panel

explanation: Handing both axes of energy management to the FMC is what allows the coded profile and speed schedule to be flown accurately.

question: What happens to the mode control panel speed window in VNAV?

options.text: It reverts to Mach indication only
It displays the current airspeed
It blanks, because the FMC is controlling the speed
It displays the FMC target speed

explanation: The blank window is the crew cue that the speed target is now in the FMC and not on the panel.

question: What does LNAV control?

options.text: Pitch, to follow the FMC vertical path
Roll, to follow the FMC route
Thrust, to follow the FMC speed schedule
Both roll and pitch

explanation: The lateral and vertical FMC functions are separate modes, so one can be used without the other.

question: If LNAV is armed before takeoff, at what point does it engage?

options.text: At 50 ft AGL
At 400 ft AGL
At 1000 ft AGL
At acceleration altitude

explanation: Engagement is delayed until the airplane is safely airborne. Verify the exact height against your operator FCOM.

question: What prevents LNAV from engaging in flight?

options.text: Having the flight directors switched off
A bank angle limit selection below 20 degrees
Having the autothrottle disengaged
Being too far from the active leg of the route

explanation: Engaging from a large displacement would command an aggressive intercept, so the logic requires the airplane to be reasonably close to the path.

question: What does the flight director command initially when the takeoff mode is selected on the ground?

options.text: A fixed pitch attitude
The pitch limit for the current flap setting
Wings level with zero pitch
The pitch required for V2 immediately

explanation: A fixed initial attitude gives a repeatable rotation target before there is enough speed information to command a speed.

question: After liftoff, to what does the takeoff flight director pitch command change?

options.text: A fixed 20 degree attitude
The FMC vertical path
A speed based command referenced to V2
The vertical speed existing at liftoff

explanation: Once airborne the priority becomes achieving and holding the climb speed, including after an engine failure.

question: What is the effect of the first push of a go around switch in flight?

options.text: The autopilot disengages
Go around mode engages with reduced go around thrust
The flaps retract to the go around setting
Full go around thrust is applied immediately

explanation: Reduced thrust is normally sufficient and gives a more controllable pitch change, with full thrust available on demand.

question: What is achieved by a second push of the go around switch?

options.text: The flight directors are removed from view
The autothrottle disengages
The mode reverts to approach
Full go around thrust is commanded

explanation: The two stage logic lets the crew ask for maximum performance when the reduced setting is not enough, such as with an engine failure or windshear.

question: Which of the following is an autothrottle mode?

options.text: THR HLD
LVL CHG
ALT ACQ
VOR/LOC

explanation: The autothrottle modes describe what the thrust levers are doing, separately from the pitch and roll modes of the autopilot.

question: At what speed during the takeoff roll does the autothrottle annunciate THR HLD?

options.text: 60 kt
84 kt
100 kt
V1

explanation: The transition happens once the takeoff thrust is established and the roll is committed. Verify the figure against your operator FCOM.

question: At what height does the THR HLD annunciation change to ARM?

options.text: 200 ft radio altitude
400 ft radio altitude
1000 ft radio altitude
Acceleration altitude

explanation: The change coincides with the height at which the autopilot may be engaged and the climb is established. Verify against your operator FCOM.

question: What is the purpose of the THR HLD mode?

options.text: It limits thrust to the reduced takeoff setting
It holds the thrust levers immovable until 400 ft
It maintains thrust after an engine failure
It prevents the autothrottle from changing thrust during the takeoff and initial climb

explanation: The thrust setting is left alone at the most critical moment, while the crew retains the ability to move the levers manually.

question: Where are the autothrottle disengage switches located?

options.text: On the thrust levers
On the mode control panel only
On the centre pedestal beside the flap lever
On the control wheels

explanation: Placing them on the levers means the hand already on the thrust is the hand that disconnects it.

question: How is an autothrottle disengagement annunciated?

options.text: By a flashing amber light
By a flashing red light
By the master caution only
By an aural warning only

explanation: The amber level reflects that losing the autothrottle is less immediately critical than losing the autopilot, but still requires attention.

question: Which autothrottle mode reduces thrust during the landing flare?

options.text: THR HLD
RETARD
ARM
N1

explanation: Bringing the levers to idle at the right moment is part of the automatic landing sequence and is annunciated so the crew can monitor it.

question: In N1 mode, what determines the thrust setting?

options.text: The N1 limit calculated by the FMC
The engine EGT limit
The position of the mode control panel speed window
The thrust lever angle selected by the crew

explanation: The FMC computes the limit for the phase and conditions, and the autothrottle simply drives the levers to achieve it.

question: What is the difference between MCP SPD and FMC SPD?

options.text: The speed target comes from the mode control panel in one and from the FMC in the other
One controls indicated airspeed and the other controls Mach
One is available with the autopilot engaged and the other is not
One is used in the climb and the other in the descent

explanation: Knowing which source owns the target tells the crew where to make a speed change.

question: With the autopilot in ALT HOLD and the autothrottle engaged, what does the autothrottle control?

options.text: Vertical speed
The N1 limit only
Airspeed
Nothing, it reverts to ARM

explanation: With pitch committed to holding the altitude, thrust is the only remaining means of controlling speed.

question: What does selecting APP mode arm?

options.text: The glideslope only
The localizer, glideslope and rollout simultaneously
The localizer only
Both the localizer and the glideslope

explanation: Arming both allows the normal capture sequence to run without further crew action.

question: In which order are the ILS beams normally captured?

options.text: Localizer first, then glideslope
Both simultaneously at the final approach fix
Either order depending on the intercept
Glideslope first, then localizer

explanation: Capturing the lateral path first ensures the airplane is aligned with the runway before it commits to the vertical path.

question: Why should APP mode not be selected until the approach is established or cleared?

options.text: Because it disengages the autothrottle
Because the system may capture a false or spurious beam
Because it blanks the speed window
Because it prevents the flaps from extending

explanation: Arming early exposes the system to side lobes and to a signal that is not yet stable, which can produce an unwanted capture.

question: During a dual channel approach, below what radio altitude does the flare mode arm?

options.text: 500 ft
800 ft

explanation: Arming well before it is needed allows the system to be monitored during the final stages. Verify the figure against your operator FCOM.

question: At approximately what radio altitude does the flare mode engage?

options.text: 20 ft
50 ft
100 ft
150 ft

explanation: The flare is initiated close to the runway so the round out and touchdown are consistent. Verify against your operator FCOM.

question: What does the rollout mode do after touchdown?

options.text: It deploys the speedbrakes and reversers
It applies the autobrakes to the selected setting
It holds the nose wheel off the runway
It uses rudder and nose wheel steering to track the localizer

explanation: Directional guidance after touchdown is the part of a low visibility landing that the crew cannot fly visually.

question: What must the crew do with the autopilot after an automatic landing?

options.text: Select CWS before leaving the runway
Nothing, it disengages at touchdown
Disengage it manually
Nothing, it disengages at taxi speed

explanation: It remains engaged through the rollout, so a positive crew action is required before manual steering is taken up.

question: What does a fail passive automatic landing system mean?

options.text: A failure is annunciated but the landing must be continued
The system reverts to a single channel and completes the landing
A failure results in disengagement without a significant out of trim condition
The system continues the landing after any single failure

explanation: Fail passive protects the airplane from a large upset on disconnect, but it does not guarantee the landing can be completed automatically.

question: Below approximately 800 ft radio altitude in a dual channel approach, what is the effect of control column force?

options.text: It reverts the autothrottle to ARM
It disengages both channels immediately
It causes a reversion to CWS in pitch
It does not cause a reversion to CWS

explanation: The reversion is inhibited so that an inadvertent nudge on the column cannot degrade the approach at its most critical stage.

question: How is the stabiliser trimmed with the autopilot engaged?

options.text: It is locked out until the autopilot is disengaged
Automatically by the autopilot
Manually by the crew using the trim switches
By the speed trim system only

explanation: Automatic trimming keeps the airplane close to trim, which is what limits the out of trim condition at disengagement.

question: How many course selectors are provided on the mode control panel?

options.text: One shared by both pilots
Two, one for each navigation receiver in use
Two, one for each pilot
Three, including a standby selector

explanation: Independent selectors allow each pilot to display a different course and support independent cross checking of the approach.

question: What happens to the flight director command bars when the autopilot is engaged in CMD with the flight directors off?

options.text: The autopilot reverts to CWS
The autopilot disengages
The autopilot continues to fly the selected modes normally
The modes revert to basic pitch and roll hold

explanation: The flight director is a display of the same computed commands, so switching it off changes what the pilot sees rather than what the autopilot does.

question: What is the effect of a single flight control computer failure?

options.text: Both autopilot channels are lost
The remaining channel can still be engaged, but a dual channel approach is not available
The autothrottle is also lost
Only CWS remains available

explanation: The redundancy is real for normal operation, and what is lost is the capability that depends on having both computers.

question: What is the consequence of losing both flight control computers?

options.text: The airplane must be flown manually
CWS remains available on both channels
The FMC takes over autopilot functions
The autothrottle continues to control both pitch and thrust

explanation: Every autopilot mode, including CWS, is computed in those units, so their loss is a total loss of autoflight.

question: In a VNAV climb, what happens if the mode control panel altitude is not raised?

options.text: The airplane levels off at the selected altitude
VNAV continues the climb to the FMC cruise altitude
The autopilot disengages at the selected altitude
VNAV reverts to LVL CHG

explanation: The panel altitude is always the hard limit, which is what makes it the primary protection against an altitude bust.

question: Which mode allows the autopilot to capture and track a VOR radial?

options.text: APP
HDG SEL
VOR/LOC
LNAV

explanation: It is a raw data mode using the navigation receiver directly, independent of the FMC route.

question: What is required before the glideslope can be captured?

options.text: The flaps must be in the landing configuration
The second autopilot channel must be engaged
The autothrottle must be in SPEED mode
The localizer must be captured

explanation: The sequence prevents the airplane from descending on the vertical path while still displaced laterally from the runway.

question: What does the autothrottle do in a LVL CHG descent?

options.text: It maintains the climb N1 limit
It retards the thrust to idle
It holds the speed with thrust
It disengages automatically

explanation: Idle thrust with pitch controlling speed is what produces the descent, mirroring the logic used in the climb.

question: Why is the autothrottle normally left engaged after an engine failure in the 737?

options.text: Because it prevents the autopilot from disengaging
Because it re-lights the failed engine automatically
Because it automatically compensates for the asymmetric thrust
Because it continues to manage thrust on the operating engine while the crew handles the failure

explanation: The autothrottle reduces workload on the remaining engine, but it does nothing about asymmetry, which remains a rudder task for the crew.

question: What does the mode annunciation on the primary flight display show?

options.text: The autopilot channel currently engaged
The active and armed autopilot, flight director and autothrottle modes
The FMC route legs in sequence
Only the modes selected on the mode control panel

explanation: The annunciation is the record of what the automation is actually doing, which is why mode awareness is checked against it rather than against the selections made.

question: What does an armed mode annunciation indicate?

options.text: The mode has failed and is unavailable
The mode will engage automatically when its capture conditions are met
The mode is selected but inhibited by the flight director
The mode is currently controlling the airplane

explanation: Distinguishing armed from active is what prevents the classic error of believing the airplane is already following a path it has not yet captured.

question: Why is monitoring the autothrottle mode as important as monitoring the pitch mode?

options.text: Because the pitch mode cannot be annunciated without it
Because the autothrottle can override the pitch mode
Because the autothrottle sets the bank angle limit
Because the pitch mode determines which of the two is controlling speed

explanation: Speed is controlled either by pitch or by thrust depending on the pitch mode, so the pair has to be read together to know where the speed protection lies.
